title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 13: Upholding Popular Sovereignty in Election Cases
keywords: Upholding Popular Sovereignty in Election Cases
Section 77 of the Omnibus Election Code
Section 44 of the Local Government Code
This one may really be for Ripley
primary_topics: Chapter 13 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- CJP's dissent in Miranda v. Comelec, where the Court voided the victory of Joel G. Miranda, who had won by 1,666 votes, and installed as mayor of Santiago City a vice mayor whom nobody had voted for as mayor

His charge of doctrinal inconsistency: barely three and a half months after Loong v. Comelec solemnly declared that upholding the sovereignty of the people is what democracy is all about, the Court abandoned that doctrine in Miranda

The legal knot he rejects -- the majority's reading that because the father's certificate of candidacy was 'cancelled' rather than one of the three grounds listed in Section 77 of the Election Code, no substitution was possible, applying expressio unius est exclusio alterius

His interpretive creed for election cases: when a reversal of the popular choice is possible, the Court must exert utmost effort to give effect to the people's will, liberally construing election laws rather than letting a confusing Comelec resolution thwart the electorate
sub_topics: He opens by quoting Loong v. Comelec's declaration that upholding the sovereignty of the people is what democracy is all about, and says the Court closed its eyes to it three and a half months later in Miranda
He lays out the facts: Jose 'Pempe' Miranda, incumbent mayor, filed his certificate of candidacy on March 24, 1998 for the May 11, 1998 elections

He notes that on Abaya's petition to deny due course to or cancel that certificate, the Comelec First Division on May 5, 1998 resolved to DISQUALIFY the elder Miranda, and that no motion for reconsideration or appeal was filed, so the Resolution became final

He recounts that Joel G. Miranda filed his own certificate the next day as substitute for his father and then won, undisputedly garnering 22,002 votes against Abaya's 20,336 -- a 1,666-vote majority that made the people's choice unquestionable
He describes Abaya's post-election petition to declare Joel Miranda's certificate null and void, which the Comelec en banc granted, nullifying his electoral victory

He summarizes the majority opinion of Justice Jose A.R. Melo: Section 77 allows substitution only for death, withdrawal or disqualification, so a merely cancelled certificate admits no substitute, and a person without a valid certificate is no candidate at all

He notes the second holding: under Nolasco v. Comelec the second placer Abaya could not be proclaimed, so Section 44 of the Local Government Code required the vice mayor to succeed to a permanent vacancy

He states his dissent, conceding that the Comelec Resolution was less than perfect, even confusing or contradictory, but insisting that such confusion must not be used to thwart the will of the electorate

He argues that sound public policy requires electoral offices to be filled by the choice of the electorate, and that election laws and jurisprudence must be liberally construed to give life to the people's mandate
He turns the majority's own recent words against it, citing Loong's exhortation that the people's will should not be kicked away by a literal interpretation of the law

He quotes the en banc Decision in Frivaldo v. Comelec framing the case as a choice of philosophy -- literal or liberal, the letter or the spirit, legal syllogism or substantial justice -- and its maxim that it is far better to err in favor of popular sovereignty
He concludes that imposing on the electorate of Santiago City a vice mayor they never voted for as mayor is an unwarranted imposition on the people and an assault on the judicial conscience

He reproduces part of the longer seventeen-page dissent of Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero, to whom the case had first been raffled, which argued that what Section 77 replaces is the disqualified candidate, not the certificate, and that Joel Miranda validly substituted for his father as the LAMMP nominee

He lets Romero answer the procedural objections as well: the five-day reglementary period could not be enforced so as to leave the substitute able to file only on election day, and the missing sworn attestation on the certificate of nomination was a harmless irregularity, since election rules are mandatory before but directory after the election

stances.claim: The Court abandoned its own freshly announced doctrine of popular sovereignty, installing as mayor of Santiago City a vice mayor whom nobody had voted for that office -- an unwarranted imposition on the people.
stances.rhetorical_move: inconsistency charge dated to the month, quoting Loong's own perorations back at the majority and topping it with a Ripley flourish

stances.claim: The Comelec's May 5, 1998 Resolution, however confusing or contradictory, disqualified the elder Miranda, so his son could validly substitute for him; the confusion should not be used to defeat a 1,666-vote majority.
stances.rhetorical_move: conceding the defect in the record, then denying it any power to reverse the electorate

stances.claim: In every action that could reverse the popular electoral choice, the Court must exert utmost effort to give effect to the people's will, liberally construing election laws rather than resolving the case by legal syllogism.
stances.rhetorical_move: elevating a rule of construction into a judicial duty, anchored on the Frivaldo passage contrasting the letter with the spirit

stances.claim: Justice Romero was right that Section 77 replaces the disqualified candidate rather than his certificate, and that formal defects such as an unattested certificate of nomination are harmless irregularities that cannot nullify an expressed sovereign choice.
stances.rhetorical_move: reinforcement by co-dissent, quoting a colleague's longer opinion in place of restating the technical argument

notable_anecdotes: He remarks that a ruling installing as mayor someone nobody voted for as mayor 'may really be for Ripley,' and that the ink in Loong had barely dried when the Court reversed course.

He records the raw arithmetic of the disputed election -- 22,002 votes for Joel Miranda against 20,336 for Abaya -- as the fact the legal reasoning had to overcome.
He points out the absurdity in the timing objection: enforcing the five-day period strictly would have let the substitute file his certificate only on election day itself.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' set CJP's dissent in Miranda v. Comelec against the Court's own recent declaration in Loong v. Comelec that upholding the sovereignty of the people is what democracy is all about. He recounted that Jose 'Pempe' Miranda, incumbent mayor of Santiago City, Isabela, filed his certificate of candidacy on March 24, 1998; that on Antonio M. Abaya's petition the Comelec First Division on May 5, 1998 resolved to disqualify him, a ruling that became final for want of appeal; that his son Joel G. Miranda filed the next day as substitute and then won the May 11 election with 22,002 votes to Abaya's 20,336; and that Abaya nevertheless persuaded the Comelec en banc to nullify the victory. Speaking through Justice Jose A.R. Melo, the Court agreed, holding that Section 77 of the Election Code permits substitution only for death, withdrawal or disqualification, that a merely cancelled certificate leaves no candidate to substitute for under expressio unius est exclusio alterius, and that since the second placer could not be proclaimed under Nolasco, Section 44 of the Local Government Code required the vice mayor to succeed. CJP said he could not in conscience accept that reasoning. He conceded that the Comelec Resolution was less than perfect, even confusing or contradictory, but insisted that such confusion should not be used to thwart the will of the electorate, that sound public policy requires offices to be filled by the choice of the voters, and that election laws must be liberally construed to give fullest effect to the people's mandate. He quoted Loong's own warning against kicking away the people's will by a literal reading of the law, and the en banc decision in Frivaldo v. Comelec framing the question as a choice between the letter and the spirit and concluding that it is far better to err in favor of popular sovereignty than to be right in little understood legalisms. Imposing on Santiago City a vice mayor nobody had voted for as mayor was, he wrote, an unwarranted imposition on the people. He closed by quoting the longer dissent of Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero, who argued that Section 77 replaces the disqualified candidate rather than his certificate and that formal defects in the certificate of nomination were harmless irregularities that could not nullify a sovereign choice.
